title: Trying to generate game assets with AI
author: Puzzleheaded_Box2842
selftext:
We’ve been exploring how to connect AI asset generation to a game development workflow, from reference images to meshes, rigging, animation, and engine import.

The approach is to split the work into smaller, replaceable stages:

* **Images to 3D:** Prepare reference images or character T-poses, then generate meshes through backends such as Meshy, Tripo, or local TRELLIS.2, with GLB output.
* **Rigging and motion:** Use Puppeteer for skeleton and skinning prediction, MoMask for text-driven human motion, and retargeting to connect motion to characters.
* **Audio and cinematics:** Separate pipelines handle dialogue, sound effects, and CG clips, so each asset type can use a suitable backend.
* **Review and integration:** Check structure, then review rendered previews and in-game behavior for scale, facing, attachments, clipping, and animation.

Underneath, model wrappers handle inference, task operators process inputs and save artifacts, and pipeline runners handle batches and metadata. This lets us change a generation backend without rewriting the whole workflow.

The important limitation is that a generated file still needs review. Motion and scene generation remain less reliable, and licensed assets can be a more practical fallback. The workflow includes visual checks and playtesting rather than treating a successful export as the finish line.

If you’ve tried a similar pipeline, which part has needed the most manual cleanup: mesh quality, rigging, retargeting, or engine integration?

This is the design we’re building in [GameFactory-3A](https://github.com/OpenDCAI/GameFactory-3A), and we’d welcome a discussion about the approach.

comments.author: Tiny_Original3761
comments.body:
For us engine integration has been the biggest time sink, and it's mostly the same handful of checks every time a model comes in:

- Facing and scale. Generated GLBs don't agree on forward axis or units. We keep every placeholder facing +Z with a size in metres, scale each model to that size (characters by height), sit it on the ground, and render it next to its placeholder to confirm it faces the same way. Redo this whenever a model is regenerated: a new version can come out facing another way.
- Don't trust the stored bounds. Recompute the bounding box before you measure anything.
- Animation names drift. The exported clip names often aren't the ones you picked (e.g. defeat_02 coming out as defeat_03), so list the clips actually in the file and match by closest name instead of hardcoding.
- Segmented models. Mesh order changes between files, so match parts by node name. Every piece keeps the whole model's origin, so move its pivot to the hinge before rotating it.
- Arm clipping. Library animations ignore body shape, so on chunky characters the arms sink into the hips or chest. Testing arm vertices against the body in every frame (winding-number test, T-pose as zero) caught far more than eyeballing thumbnails; the fix is turning the upper arm out at the shoulder after each frame.
- "In place" clips can still drift the hips; centre them over the whole clip.
